items.question: Why do you think making the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus challenge a target for the AI research community is a terrible idea?
items.object: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus challenge as a community research target
items.answer: It's a terrible idea. That's not what it's supposed to be. It's not supposed to be something where we then design methods to solve the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus challenge.

items.question: How do you think the control of AI should serve the public?
items.object: AI ownership, public benefit, and the alignment of power
items.answer: Fundamentally, AI is trained on the collective outputs of humanity. This technology belongs to everyone. Centralized resources in the interest of the common good, in the interest of the public, and not in the interest of maximum profit. Because to me, the biggest alignment challenge is not between AI and humans. Biggest alignment challenge is between those people who hold the keys to power and control the systems and the rest of the population.

items.question: How do you describe the research focus of your AI lab at the University of Oxford?
items.object: The research agenda of Jakob Foerster's AI lab at the University of Oxford
items.answer: I run the first lab for AI research at the University of Oxford, which is nowadays about 30 people working on anything that is cutting edge, interesting, not supervised learning, thinking beyond current state of the art.

items.question: Why do you think deep reinforcement learning has fallen short of its potential for real-world impact?
items.object: Deep reinforcement learning’s hardware lottery
items.answer: So I think reinforcement learning in the last decade or so really hasn't lived up to its potential, which raised a question: why is it that deep learning has been this revolutionary success story where deep reinforcement learning, which held that great promise, really hasn't quite delivered in terms of real world impact? And we have a hypothesis at Foerster Lab for AI Research, which is that deep reinforcement learning had lost the hardware lottery because deep learning is perfectly suited for the GPU. We can really keep all the cores busy churning through data efficiently. In contrast, the way that deep reinforcement learning has been done in the field is running reinforcement learning environments on the CPU, but running the agents on the GPU. And this has meant all sorts of complications and complexity, both in algorithm design and in terms of hardware we need and how we're going to develop algorithms for this, which has really slowed down the field. And this meant experimentation, very slow and difficult. And we're currently in this revolution really, which is for the first time allowing us to run environments and agents together jointly on the GPU, making deep reinforcement learning finally a winner in the hardware lottery. And then hopefully this will be the step to really making reinforcement learning work in the real world.

items.question: Why do you think reinforcement learning algorithms have been so brittle?
items.object: The brittleness of reinforcement learning algorithms
items.answer: I think what has happened is because experimentation has been so slow, we've only been able to train our algorithms on very specific environments, and we've only been able to hill climb on that very small set of environments, which means the things are fundamentally brittle. And now, for the first time, the experimental loop has been sped up by orders of magnitude, which means that now we can really start to develop methods that are robust. Remember, the scientists we are, we ourselves are doing meta learning. We're trying to discover methods that can generalize.

items.question: How do you think the cost of experimentation affects the quality of deep reinforcement learning methods?
items.object: The cost of experimentation in deep reinforcement learning
items.answer: We have to be able to actually get a lot of samples and get a lot of experience for how our methods actually work. And in deep reinforcement learning, any single run has taken a lot of cost, a lot of compute, and a lot of time. And that means the signal we are getting as researchers has been costly, has been sparse, and has been noisy, and that meant our methods are bad. And the premise is from the bitter lesson. If we can churn through more data, we can get a better signal, get better gradient updates for either the researchers or our meta learning methods to then optimize our algorithms to be more robust, more efficient in the real world.

items.question: How do you frame the challenge of learning when real-world experience is expensive?
items.object: Learning when real-world experience is expensive
items.answer: So I think this is a general problem, which is what happens when real world experience is expensive. And obviously we've been really good as a field at using real world data when it's given to us.
quotes: So I think this is a general problem, which is what happens when real world experience is expensive. And obviously we've been really good as a field at using real world data when it's given to us.

items.question: How do you see compute-only scaling helping machine learning progress as real-world data becomes harder to obtain?
items.object: Compute-only scaling through fast, approximate simulations
items.answer: So we've been in this regime where we could lazily scale up compute and data, because data sets were large enough to be accommodating for small amounts of compute. But now we're hitting the data wall. And the question then is, if I can't get more data from the real world, how can I use simulation in environments that are not perfect and not exactly the same as the real world, but are blazing fast and allow me to get a lot more data in a way that's fully synthetic? And that's really, I think, one of the key questions right now for the field, not just for reinforcement learning. How can I develop algorithms, discover algorithms in approximate versions, for example, of data that run 10,000 times faster in a way that then the algorithms we discover will generalize to the real data environment, which is slow, which is expensive to run? And I put this under the umbrella of compute only scaling. If you just give me tons and tons of compute, what kind of methods can I develop that will allow me to make progress on the simulated situations, environment scenarios, so that the learning progress transfers to downstream tasks in the real world that are slow and expensive to run.

items.question: What do you see as the value of faster reinforcement learning experiments for algorithm design?
items.object: Faster reinforcement learning experiments and algorithm simplicity
items.answer: It's not just being able to do experiments that the big boys could do, but we couldn't do. It's also being able to simplify algorithms, right? It's being able to take out a lot of the complexity that was built in and makes it difficult to understand what these algorithms are doing. And being able to say, let's actually just write these very clean algorithms. So we have this paper from our lab on parallelized Q-learning. It's just extraordinarily simple. It's basically just a Q learner where a lot of different agents across different cores step through the environment and learn on every transition.

items.question: How do you think removing target networks and replay buffers could shape the future of reinforcement learning algorithms?
items.object: Simplifying reinforcement learning algorithms by removing target networks and replay buffers
items.answer: No more target networks, no more replay buffers. And all of this is gone. And I think that just hopefully will allow the field to come up with much more beautiful and understandable and therefore robust algorithms in the future.

items.question: What did you find valuable about Mirror Learning as a framework for reinforcement learning?
items.object: Mirror Learning and learned drift functions
items.answer: We had a paper that was called Mirror Learning that basically provided a theoretical framework that, to me at least, provided the first intuitive understanding of why things like PPO actually work. And what this framework said is, as long as we have a penalty term that penalizes difference between the policy that collected the data and our current updated policy that obeys certain properties, then we will, in the limit of doing many policy updates, converge to an optimal policy. The theory framework was really nice, but what it also allowed us to do is to say, why don't we learn a drift function? Because PPO, that clip, is just one of many possible algorithms that can be expressed in the mirror learning space. And we thought, well, maybe this isn't the optimal one. There must be better ones. So what then we set out to do is to parameterize this drift function as neural networks.

items.question: How do you assess evolution strategies as a way to optimize through an entire reinforcement learning loop?
items.object: Evolution strategies for optimizing through reinforcement learning
items.answer: There's been a lot of work in the field on meta gradient estimation, and there was always trying to estimate this sort of derivative by unrolling the computation graph and differentiating through it. And actually I've done some of this work in my PhD, coming out of the multi-agent shaping work again. And we pursued this path because that's what everyone thought was going to win. But then we also pursued evolution strategies, which does not do any of the sophisticated maths, but instead swallows the bitter lesson and doubles down on it by just doing black box optimization, trying to estimate those high order derivatives from samples. And that turned out to be extremely well suited for the new paradigm of RL at the hyperscale.

items.question: What did you find interesting about the clipping behavior of the reinforcement learning objective you meta-learned?
items.object: The meta-learned reinforcement learning objective’s clipping behavior
items.answer: So the interesting thing is it recovered some of the features that we had seen in PPO. So there is this clip-like behavior, but there are a few aspects that were novel. So for example, the clip counter-intuitively maybe has this sort of too-good-to-be-true type of behavior where you're okay to update to have a positive gradient if you're beyond the clip region, as long as your advantage isn't too high. So you would actually think intuitively, if I have a large advantage, if things turned out much better than I thought, I should be more optimistic and go way further from the reference policy. But instead this clip function does the opposite, where if the advantage is high and you've moved away further, then you have to stop there. But if the advantage is small, then you can move further away from the reference policy.

items.question: How do you understand the rollback behavior that DPO discovered compared with the PPO objective?
items.object: Rollback behavior discovered by DPO compared with the PPO objective
items.answer: The other thing that this process discovered, that we then realized had actually been discovered by humans before, is rollback. So while the PPO objective says if you have gone too far away from the reference policy and you have a negative advantage, you're not going to get a gradient, you're going to stay there in that lower left quadrant. Instead, DPO discovered you should actually go back. We're going to push you back to that reference policy.

The response states that DPO's rollback pushes the policy back toward the reference policy when it has moved too far away and the advantage is negative.

items.question: Why did you consider it important to have a human interpret a discovered learning algorithm and express its drift function symbolically?
items.object: Human interpretation and symbolic representation of a discovered learning algorithm’s drift function
items.answer: So I think the hope here is that ultimately, at that point, we hadn't yet transitioned to let's just do science end to end with AI agents. So having the human in the loop who can interpret this and get back a symbolic representation of the drift function was really important to us. It has a second advantage, which is then suddenly you can break out of the box. Remember, the environments we're going to use in Jax will not be the real world. We can't implement every problem. But I think what we can do is we can have a representative set of types of challenges that make the learning algorithms that we discover transfer to the real world, transfer to settings in other simulators, and also to learn world models. And having a symbolic representation, we can just write down that drift function in one line of Python, which is a really nice way to make sure it transfers to different downstream tasks and to other code environments.

items.question: How do you see the value of meta optimization for designing time-dependent clip functions in DPO?
items.object: Meta optimization of time-dependent clip functions in DPO
items.answer: What we've done in follow-up work is we've said, fine, so humans can design these clip functions. But something that humans certainly can't do is design a clip function that is time dependent, with time being how far into the optimization process the learning algorithm is. And this sort of temporally aware version of DPO turned out to be very explicit about trading off exploration early on, with then becoming more conservative along the path of the optimization process. And obviously this is a huge design space because now designing a clip function for every process in time, and this is again where meta optimization shines. The only thing we haven't been able to do in that case is to go back and say, can we find a parametric version of this kind of clip function manifold?

items.object: LLM-guided search over programs for discovering reinforcement learning algorithms
items.answer: I think this is something we are starting to explore. We've done a few papers now at Foerster Lab for AI Research and a few works in progress, which is rather than using black box function approximators, let's explore in the space of programs, and again use Jax at the hyperscale to get relatively fast feedback on the different members, and then use LLMs as the mutation operator to explore in the space of programs using the fitness, which is the performance on the downstream tasks of the reinforcement learning algorithm that we're exploring, as the mutation signal. I think this opens up an entire new space of automated reinforcement learning, as we discussed before, which then obviously makes the question of how do we prevent this from overfitting even more important?

items.question: How do you think about the risk of benchmark overfitting as reinforcement learning research becomes automated?
items.object: Goodhart's law and generalization in automated reinforcement learning research
items.answer: So there's Goodhart's law, which says if the measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. And this already has happened when we do science with, like, graduate student descent, use law of exploration and trials and errors to optimize our benchmarks. But now imagine if we can scale this up by automated research. So this is something else we've been talking about a lot at Foerster Lab for AI Research, which is how do we make sure that the algorithmic progress we find in the meta loop actually transfers downstream. What's the right framework to think about meta train and meta test? Along what axis should we be generalizing? How do we know that this is real?

items.question: How do you think the AI research community should use the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus challenge to guide progress?
items.object: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus challenge as a measure and target of AI progress
items.answer: I think the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus challenge as a measure of progress is brilliant. It shows that our systems are lacking fundamental capabilities, but the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus challenge as a target for the community is a terrible idea, because that's not what it's supposed to be. It's not supposed to be something where we then design methods to solve the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus challenge. And this is where open-endedness comes in. We'd like to have methods that can solve a broad range of diverse tasks, and the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus challenge is one example in that space, which means we have to target the entire space of human solvable problems.

items.question: How do you think the AI research community should use benchmarks such as the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus to make progress on human-level reasoning?
items.object: Benchmarks as measures versus targets for progress in human-level reasoning
items.answer: There's two answers. One is, as a community, be much more clear about measures and targets because we use the term benchmark. But a benchmark is supposed to be a measure, not a target. And what this means in practice is we have to work much more clearly on addressing broader problem spaces and then just having the benchmarks be one instance in that entire open space of problems, and never use the benchmark during the development process of our methodologies. What this would mean is I am working not on Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus, but I'm working on human level reasoning capabilities. And in my entire pipeline of methods, of design, of training, I never use Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus. I only use it once a year to measure my progress. And I'm not just using Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus. I'm using other examples like Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus where LLMs struggle, where humans can make progress. That's one option. And the other option is rather than having unique benchmarks that we can use to measure the target we generate, we make benchmark design a first class member of our scientific progress, which means we're trying to generate benchmarks that span the entire space of problems. Which means then if you hill climb this entire space of problems, you are hill climbing all of human capabilities. And I think we haven't made that much progress on the latter. So I think for now, just being very clear about the measure and the target in the community is super, super important.
quotes: There's two answers. One is, as a community, be much more clear about measures and targets because we use the term benchmark. But a benchmark is supposed to be a measure, not a target. And what this means in practice is we have to work much more clearly on addressing broader problem spaces and then just having the benchmarks be one instance in that entire open space of problems, and never use the benchmark during the development process of our methodologies.

What this would mean is I am working not on Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus, but I'm working on human level reasoning capabilities. And in my entire pipeline of methods, of design, of training, I never use Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus. I only use it once a year to measure my progress. And I'm not just using Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus. I'm using other examples like Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus where LLMs struggle, where humans can make progress.

That's one option. And the other option is rather than having unique benchmarks that we can use to measure the target we generate, we make benchmark design a first class member of our scientific progress, which means we're trying to generate benchmarks that span the entire space of problems. Which means then if you hill climb this entire space of problems, you are hill climbing all of human capabilities. And I think we haven't made that much progress on the latter. So I think for now, just being very clear about the measure and the target in the community is super, super important.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between creativity and reasoning in your research?
items.object: The relationship between creativity and reasoning
items.answer: I think creativity allows at least me to come up with new reasoning challenges. If I think about how I go about my day, it's commonly using creativity to try and create new problems for myself and frankly, for the lab and for the research community, and then also explore the space of solutions. And one of the skills that I need in solving these problems is then reasoning, right? So it's basically allowing me or researchers in general, I think, to explore space of interesting and relevant problems that can then be used to train our reasoning capabilities, much like curriculum design. So I think creativity is a great driver for figuring out what problems are interesting. And I think this is one of the key challenges right now for open-endedness, which is what actually constitutes an interesting problem, because obviously if we just rely on LLMs, we're going to make the measure the target. We will start Goodharting the judgment of LLMs.

items.question: How do you judge whether searching for a solution, as in playing chess, is a creative process?
items.object: Creativity in problem-solving search
items.answer: I probably would argue that it depends on how structured your search space is. So for example, to me, playing chess the way that a human does it has a strong flavor of creativity because you can't simulate trillions of time steps. You have to solve this problem differently. You have to actually try and find an intuitive approach to it that finds unusual new pathways and patterns. And that sounds creative. If I look at the way that this was solved in the Goodharted way of doing AI for games in the past, it's quite brute force. That's effectively just number crunching the game, and that doesn't seem very creative to me.

items.question: How do you see the distinction between using chess as a measure and using it as a target in AI research?
items.object: Chess as a measure versus a target in AI research
items.answer: So I think it's less about what are we doing, but how are we doing it. Which goes back to measuring the target. Because if I use chess as a measure, then I only get a human compatible number of samples. I can't just brute force or number crunch the game. I have to be creative. I have to explore. I have to play. I have to use imagination. But if I'm allowed to use this game as a target, like DeepMind did it, and of course this was great work at the time, but the methods haven't really transferred to other domains, then suddenly I can turn these beautiful imagination problems into number crunching.

items.question: How do you see using computation at the meta level helping AI generalize to new situations?
items.object: Using computation at the meta level to discover sample-efficient learning algorithms
items.answer: I think my hope is that if we use the fact that we can number crunch, but we're not going to number crunch specific policies for specific problems, but we're going to use number crunching for finding, sharpening our intuition about algorithms and about sample efficient methods, about methods that can use imagination, that could plan on new domains, that can explore. Then we will have the best of both worlds. We will use the compute. We will use the efficient samples that we can get, but we will not use them to overfit on specific problems, but to sharpen our intuitions and to automate scientific discovery and accelerate the exploration of extremely sample efficient algorithms that then hopefully can have human like capabilities. Because my mental model is the reason that we are so sample efficient is because we're the result of an extraordinarily sample inefficient process called evolution. We've been optimized on this evolutionary time scale with vast sampling efficiency, but now allowed us to have this final product, which is a meta learned agent that can deal with new situations, come to a recording studio and be underslept and still vaguely make sense.

items.question: How do you think interactions with other agents give rise to intelligence?
items.object: Intelligence as an emergent phenomenon of multi-agent interactions
items.answer: I think there's been a long term hypothesis that I've been pursuing as a scientist, which is intelligence is an emergent phenomenon of multi-agent interactions, that the reason we have our capabilities of abstraction, of language, of reasoning, of communication, are because we interact in extraordinarily complicated environments where the most complex parts are not doors and bananas and apples and lions. But there are other agents like us that force us to reason over others, the theory of mind, learn from each other, teach each other, coordinate, communicate, cooperate.

items.question: How do you understand the role of increasing scales of coordination in the evolution of human intelligence and society?
items.object: The evolution of intelligence through increasing scales of coordination
items.answer: I think of it, broadly speaking, as sort of a sequence of platforms, right? Where we had originally DNA with evolution, bacteria, single cells. And that became the platform for multi-celled organisms. Multi-celled organisms became a platform for reinforcement learning, animals that could learn at test time within their lifetime. That became the platform for groups of agents to interact. And in those groups of agents, we could then develop all of the reasoning skills, the cognitive skills that really make the human species unique. So at least where have we come from? This has been a path of gradual, bigger and bigger scale of coordination. I think ultimately our society right now is at that cusp of trying to figure out what does coordination mean? What's the next step in that evolutionary process? How do we coordinate better? How do we go from, again, sort of like single cells fighting each other, individual humans being at conflict, individual nations being at conflict to greater coordination and cooperation at that bigger scale? And I think there's hints of this that we're seeing, but we also really haven't figured this out as humanity, really.

items.question: How do you understand reward hacking as a phenomenon shared by AI agents and humans?
items.object: Reward hacking in AI agents and humans
items.answer: Reward hacking is not something unique to AI agents. Humans have reward functions all the time. In fact, in my mental model, every reward is reward shaping and comes with reward hacking, right? I mean, think about p-hacking in the scientific community. That is nothing but reward hacking. The signal, which is recognition for having papers accepted. To get a paper accepted, you have to have a p-value of less than 0.05. So we don't call it reward hacking. But this is what happens everywhere. This is not something new.

items.question: How do you see the role of design choices in shaping the agency of LLM agents?
items.object: The design of agency in LLM agents
items.answer: I think the way that we're building these agents is very, very different. I think there are obviously differences in the design process leading to different properties. So for example, we've really designed LLM agents to obfuscate levels of agency, to be saying, oh, I'm just an AI agent. I can't, you know, I don't have consciousness. I don't have these properties. I don't have intentions, right? But that's a design choice, right? So in many ways we've played the role as AI scientists, designing those agents to have certain properties and pursue certain goals, much like the evolutionary process has shaped us.

items.question: How do you understand the difference between human intentionality and intentionality in AI agents?
items.object: Intentionality in humans and AI agents
items.answer: Well, I mean, we have our intentionality, in my mental model, again, as a side product of having to have goal pursuit to survive. So it's an evolutionary feature. Currently, we don't yet train AI agents from the ground up to be goal pursuing, but to be imitating. The current paradigm first and foremost is imitation based. Now we've also seen that this paradigm leads to systems which are not very good at being agentic. So I think quite a natural step down the line is to do a genetic pre-training, where we also train these agents to actually pursue goals. And at that point, I think we're much, much closer in terms of intentionality to what we do as humans, which is goal pursuit.

items.question: Why do you think strong agentic AI will require autonomy?
items.object: Autonomy in strong agentic AI
items.answer: I think it's difficult to imagine that we will have strong genetic systems that will be simple enough so they don't look like they have autonomy. Everything I can imagine around what we need to get there will be agents that can set their own goals, own subgoals, that can self improve their own learning processes, that can work together in teams of students and teachers. And it's almost sort of like a contradiction per se to have strong AI, strong agentic AI, and to have things that don't look like autonomy. Because, again, it's going to be difficult to write down an explicit learning rule or explicit data set that will get us there, right? Everything we do around self-improvement, around emergent properties of multi-agent teams, of large networks of agents, of cultural transmission, of computational self-improvement through discovering new concepts, requires these agents to have essentially autonomy.

items.question: Why do you prefer a distributed, swarm-intelligence vision of AGI to a single monolithic system?
items.object: Monolithic AGI versus distributed swarm intelligence
items.answer: I think there's two answers to this because AGI can be in principle a single entity. But I find that vision quite dystopian, that AGI is a monolithic system. And instead I much prefer the sort of swarm intelligence view on intelligence, right? Because humanity obviously we do things that no single human could do. We have this decentralized compute network of agents going about their lives and figuring out sorts of structures and rewiring themselves and new computation graphs and getting tens of thousands of people to fly to conferences to do collective computing and imagination. And to me, the intelligence is in that system, and I hope that we'll find approaches of having that same level of distributed, decentralized compute structure, but now augment it with agentic AI systems.

items.question: Why do you see multi-agent learning and multi-agent intelligence as the next frontier for AI?
items.object: Multi-agent learning and multi-agent intelligence
items.answer: I don't think anyone has quite managed to put their finger on it. So this is the funny thing. Multi-agent learning has been the future forever. But like many areas, things that have been the future forever suddenly have become reality, right? Self-driving cars were always in the future. Quantum computers were always useless. And suddenly the future is happening. And I think multi-agent learning and multi-agent intelligence is that next frontier of things that were always there, like this will be the future at some point, and now it's happening. And it gives you not just decentralization, robustness, but it also gives you this ability of effectively deploying vast amounts of test time compute, because suddenly you can also use test time compute to rewire yourself, to re-explore new solutions, to divide and conquer. And I think that's going to be extraordinarily powerful now that we have solved a lot of the first requirements to make this work. We now have agents that are good enough at basic reasoning. I think we'll get to agents that can do basic agentic behavior. And then the multi-agentic behavior, I think, will be the next emergent property or the next platform for real innovation in this space.

items.question: What did you want your paper “Risks and opportunities of open source generative AI” to contribute to the debate about open-source AI?
items.object: The paper “Risks and opportunities of open source generative AI”
items.answer: This paper goes back to a conversation I had with Phil Thor at lunch in Oxford about a year ago, and at the time, really, there hadn't been that much work in the space of open source LLMs, and we were very concerned about the accumulation of power behind the large players and the closed source AI space, because, again, to me, this decentralization of intelligence is not just a path to having smart systems that are robust, but it's also something that gives agency to the parts of this network. And it's, to me, a foundation of Western thought, Western democracy and balance of power that maintains our social structures and prevents dictatorial takeovers. And at the time, there was a lot of discussion about the risks of open source AGI. But very few people were speaking out about the benefits of open source AGI and the risks of closed source AI. So what we decided is to gather a group of people, and it came out of a workshop in London on open innovation to write a paper that would try and tell the other side of the story, which we thought was lacking in the discourse. Obviously, writing this paper took time, and the great news is that while we're even in the process of writing this paper, more and more open source systems were coming out for LLMs, which means that now I think a lot of that paper is no longer as urgent. But I still think being able to tell the story, these are the risks of AGI that are commonly ignored. And these are the benefits of decentralization, of democratization, of giving everyone access to these tools and being able to deploy them across the economy. Being able to deploy them across the planet and giving these to everyone who wants to innovate. That's the story we wanted to tell. And I think the paper does a decent job at this.

items.question: Under what conditions would you support centralizing resources for AGI development?
items.object: Centralization and democratic control of AGI development
items.answer: Centralization is one aspect, but the different question is if it's centralized, who holds the keys? What we're doing right now is we're having the Manhattan Project developed by private enterprise, funded by people from across the world, from all sorts of backgrounds and interests, that if they were funding the Manhattan Project, that would have been absurd. So I'm on board with saying we need to have centralized resources, but less centralized resources in the interest of the common good and the interest of the public and not in the interest of maximum profit. We often confound those two. I think if we had something like a CERN-style effort of pooling resources from across Europe, from across the globe, of trying to build models for the common good that are transparent, where the data that we use is public, is accessible, is curated by the public, with the alignment methods that we use again democratically vetted, come out of a sort of decentralized process like Wikipedia, where a lot of people can have input in public, in the open, transparently. I'm on board with this. I'm on board with centralization as long as it's controlled by democratic forces. The goal is the common good, because to me, the biggest alignment challenge is not between AI and humans, because the alignment challenge is between those people who hold the keys to power and control the systems and the rest of the population.

items.question: How do you assess the catastrophic risks of making dual-use AI systems open source?
items.object: Catastrophic risks of open-source dual-use AI systems
items.answer: I think the scale of what counts as catastrophic matters. So, for example, I think having open source systems that can be dual use is probably a good thing, because it will give us early signals of where things can be exploited and there can be malicious use. But if you have open source access, at some point you get the same balance of power which underlies the stability of our world. Most actors are good, and being able to use the same methods for defense will also help us early develop defenses against the abuse of this technology. These kinds of abuses by bad actors will not be the end of humanity, but the catastrophic abuse of a runaway paperclip maximizer slash profit maximizer could actually be the end of the human species, and could certainly be the end of our Western democracies. So I think we have to be very careful when we talk about catastrophic, on that scale of what that term can actually mean for different people.

These kinds of abuses by bad actors will not be the end of humanity, but the catastrophic abuse of a runaway paperclip maximizer slash profit maximizer could actually be the end of the human species, and could certainly be the end of our Western democracies. So I think we have to be very careful when we talk about catastrophic, on that scale of what that term can actually mean for different people.

The response argues that shared access to AI capabilities can create a stabilizing balance of power between attackers and defenders.
The response presents runaway AI optimization as a greater existential threat than bad-actor misuse of open-source dual-use AI.

items.question: Why do you think equal access to AI is the right approach internationally, including for countries whose intentions you distrust?
items.object: Equal access to AI across countries
items.answer: I think it's on the international scale the same that applies on the national scale, which is the balance of power. If you equalize access to tools, that balance of power between different countries needs to be maintained, and giving fair access to AI is just part of the equation. Fundamentally, AI is trained on the collective outputs of humanity. This technology belongs to everyone, including people we don't like. I think it's actually quite wrong to say only a small fraction of Western elites should have access to this, because this is trained on the cultural evolution of the output of all of humanity. So let's use it for the benefit. And the only way that I can ensure this use for the benefit is to give equal access to people.

items.question: Why do you want to go beyond open-source AGI toward what you call holistic alignment?
items.object: Holistic alignment through democratic networks of humans and AI assistants
items.answer: Personally, I would prefer to go beyond just open sourcing. In our paper we had a section on the question of open source AGI, and the argument we make in a nutshell is open source is better than closed source from a risk perspective, because it prevents the catastrophic accumulation of power and the misaligned entity. It prevents this. But even better would be systems which are holistically aligned. And what I mean by that is, imagine if you had swarm intelligence where every person had their personal AI representative that is trained for them to augment them. And the only way that we could do superintelligence is by having these teams of people and their assistants interact in a large network. And we had processes of making the mechanisms in that large network fundamentally democratic, which means the only way we can get to superintelligence is through this hybrid approach of humans and their agents, their assistants, which means this sort of distributed computing platform could never be used against the interest of the humans in it. We had long discussions about this term of holistic alignment. I said, you know what this is? This is it. We have to pursue it. Because fundamentally, the reason we're in this weird position now where everyone is racing to build something that nobody actually believes is a good thing for humanity is the coordination failure. So why don't we use AI to help us coordinate better, to build systems that are fundamentally democratic in their design, that fundamentally allow us to have a technology which cannot be abused against the humans in it, rather than to say, we're going to drive coordination failure to the maximum.

items.question: How do you think open-source AI development can overcome the enormous cost of building frontier models?
items.object: Resourcing open-source frontier AI development
items.answer: So there's two answers. In the short term, absolutely. We rely on the large industry players like Meta who are pursuing open source. And it's one of the reasons why I'm at Meta 50%, because I want to strengthen that effort. I want to help open source leapfrog closed source. So this is in the short term. I think in the long term, we need to pool resources in the common interest as a CERN-like effort. Why could we build CERN with thousands of authors? And we're not able to put the resources that go into academia into one collective effort of doing a moonshot-like project of building the best models? If you think about the collective intelligence in academia, it dwarfs anything in any of the large labs. Of course, you can have thousands of research scientists at DeepMind, but you can't have tens of thousands of brilliant young minds that we have in academia. And the interest should be such that there's enough players who don't want the monolithic future. And to me, this is a coordination challenge. And I think at one point we look back and say, why did it take us so long to realize that there's a huge opportunity here to bring together resources from a diverse set of players and try and make sure that every single PhD student, every single postdoc, every single PI can be as efficient as possible to drive forward the vision of open source AGI.

items.question: Why do you think developers who open-source AI models should not be liable for how others use them?
items.object: Liability for developers of open-source AI models
items.answer: If I open source the model, I should not be liable for what happens with that tool. Imagine a world where if you're building a hammer, you get put in jail because somebody's a bad actor, takes that hammer and intentionally causes damage. Obviously you can't produce hammers anymore, right? Instead, the only way that you could get a nail into the wall is by hiring the hammering service, which holds all the hammers in their coffins and controls. And then you have to say, well, what kind of nail are you putting into the wall? Sorry, what picture are you hanging up? So we don't like that picture. We're not going to put that nail into the wall because we don't like it. I say, well, no, it's my wall. It's my apartment. No, no, no, sorry, hammer company says no. That would be absurd. And yet, when we get to AI models, we've gotten quite accustomed to the fact that we're handing over agency. As an AI user, I have intentions. I am liable for my actions. And suddenly the computer says no, like, sorry, you're not being nice. Was this nice to whom and who says that I need to be nice to people? If I want to be annoying, I can be annoying if I ask my students. So to me, fundamentally, we've handed over agency and I think it's gonna be one of the big absurdities.

items.question: How do you view the transfer of collective intelligence infrastructure to private companies through Google Search and AI access?
items.object: Private control of collective intelligence infrastructure
items.answer: To me, fundamentally, we've handed over agency and I think it's gonna be one of the big absurdities. The fact that we collectively have given away the keys to our collective intelligence infrastructure. It started with Google Search. We used to have libraries. There was a public index. There was a fair and equal access to information. And Google Search gave away our collective hippocampus, the indexing structure, into collective memory to a for-profit entity. And now we're doing the same with AI access. It's like having a typewriter where as you're writing it once in a while, there's no, sorry, you can't say that, right? Obviously, I can type whatever I want, and I don't see a way out of this beyond open source. And maybe in the long run, these holistic alignment systems that are fundamentally built up to be democratic.
